title: A Year of Festivals and a Temple Near Chicago
bigQuestion: How do Hindu festivals and worship keep the stories of the texts alive for families today?

story.title: Shoes at the Door
story.kicker: A fourth-grade class visits a Hindu temple in Lemont, Illinois.
paragraphs: The school bus climbs a hill in Lemont, southwest of Chicago. At the top stands a white temple with carved towers. It is the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago. The class steps off the bus, and the air smells like flowers and warm oil.

A volunteer named Mrs. Rao meets them at the door. "Before we go in, we take off our shoes," she says kindly. "It shows respect, like wiping your feet at a friend's house." The students line their sneakers in neat rows. Some socks have holes, and everyone laughs quietly.

Inside, the floor is cool. Mrs. Rao leads them to a shrine where murtis of Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman stand dressed in bright cloth. A priest waves a small lamp in circles while a bell rings. Families stand with their hands pressed together.

"This is called arati," Mrs. Rao whispers. "People are showing love and respect to God." On the way out, she gives each student a small sweet in a paper cup. "This is prasad," she says. "It was offered first, and now it is shared."
story.think: The students took off their shoes and used quiet voices. Why do you think visitors show respect in these ways at a place of worship?

sections.title: A Calendar of Moon and Sun

lessons.title: Why the Dates Move
lessons.mainIdea: Most Hindu festivals follow a calendar based on both the moon and the sun, so their dates change each year.
reading: Look at a wall calendar. Diwali might fall in October one year and November the next. Why does it move? Most Hindu festivals follow a *lunar* calendar, which counts months by the moon.

A moon month runs from one new moon to the next. Twelve moon months are a little shorter than a sun year. So Hindu calendars add an extra month every few years to keep in step with the seasons. Calendars like this are called lunisolar.

India has several regional calendars, so some dates differ from place to place. A few festivals, like Pongal, follow the sun and fall on nearly the same date each year. Temples in Illinois post each year's festival dates for families.

words.d: having to do with the moon; a lunar month goes from one new moon to the next
a calendar that follows both the moon and the sun

look.title: Moon Months and Sun Years

lessons.title: Festivals Remember Stories
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindu festivals remember a story from the epics or the Puranas.
reading: Ask a Hindu family why they light lamps on Diwali, and you may hear a story. Many say the lamps welcome Rama home to Ayodhya after fourteen years. Festivals are one way families pass down the stories of the texts.

Many festival stories come from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the *Puranas*. The Puranas are long books of stories about Vishnu, Shiva, Devi and other deities. They were written down over many centuries.

One festival can remember different stories in different regions. That is normal in Hinduism. A family in Gujarat and a family in Tamil Nadu may tell different stories on the same day, and both are part of the tradition.

words.d: long Hindu books of stories about deities, creation and worship
a special day or season of celebration and worship

look.title: One Day, Two Stories
look.text: On Diwali, a family from North India tells how Rama came home to Ayodhya. A family from South India tells how Krishna defeated the demon king Narakasura. Both light lamps.
look.prompt: Why might one festival hold two different stories? What do both families share?

check.q: Why do many families light lamps on Diwali?
check.why: Many families say Diwali lamps welcome Rama home to Ayodhya.

check.q: What are the Puranas?
choices: Long books of stories about deities
check.why: The Puranas are long Hindu texts of stories about Vishnu, Shiva, Devi and others.

check.q: Is it normal for one festival to have different stories in different regions?
choices: Yes, it is normal in Hinduism
check.why: Different regions often tell different stories for the same festival.

lessons.title: Pongal: A Harvest Thank-You
lessons.mainIdea: Pongal is a Tamil harvest festival in January that gives thanks to the sun.
reading: In mid-January, a family in Tamil Nadu sets a clay pot of rice and milk on a fire. They watch until it bubbles over. Everyone shouts, "Pongalo pongal!" This is *Pongal*, a harvest festival.

Pongal gives thanks to Surya, the sun, for the harvest. The name of the festival is also the name of the sweet rice dish. The overflowing pot is a sign of plenty. Families also honor the cows and bulls that help on farms.
Tamil families in Illinois celebrate Pongal too, often in their kitchens and at temples. Other parts of India hold harvest festivals at the same time with different names, such as Makar Sankranti.

words.d: a Tamil harvest festival in January, and the sweet rice dish cooked for it
the time when crops are gathered from the fields

look.title: The Overflowing Pot
look.text: Rice, milk and sugar cook in a pot until the foam spills over the sides. The family cheers when it overflows.
look.prompt: Why do you think the pot overflowing is a happy sign at a harvest festival?

check.why: Pongal thanks Surya, the sun, for the harvest.

check.why: Pongal is a Tamil festival from Tamil Nadu in South India.

check.q: What is another name for a harvest festival held at the same time?
check.why: Makar Sankranti is celebrated in other regions around the same time as Pongal.

lessons.title: Diwali: Lights and Lakshmi
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates light over darkness with lamps, sweets and prayer.
reading: On Diwali night, rows of small clay lamps glow on windowsills. Children light sparklers. Families share sweets with neighbors. *Diwali* comes from a Sanskrit word meaning a row of lamps.

Many Hindus say Diwali celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. In the north, many remember Rama's return to Ayodhya. Many families also worship Lakshmi, the goddess of good fortune, and clean their homes to welcome her.
Diwali falls in October or November. Jains and Sikhs also mark this time, each with their own reasons. In Illinois, many towns and schools now hold Diwali events, and temples fill with families.

words.d: the Hindu festival of lights, in October or November
the Hindu goddess of good fortune and wealth, often honored on Diwali
a small clay oil lamp lit on Diwali

look.prompt: What might the lamps stand for, according to many Hindus? Use the words light and darkness.

check.q: Which goddess do many families worship on Diwali?

check.q: Which other traditions also mark this season?
check.why: Jains and Sikhs also mark this time, each with their own reasons.

lessons.title: Holi: Colors of Spring
lessons.mainIdea: Holi is a spring festival of colors that remembers the story of Prahlad and the playful love of Krishna.
reading: On Holi morning, friends chase each other with bright powders of pink, green and yellow. Soon everyone is covered in color. *Holi* comes in March, at the end of winter.

The night before, many families light a bonfire. It remembers a story from the Puranas. Prince Prahlad stayed devoted to Vishnu, even when his father tried to harm him. His aunt Holika tried to burn him, but Prahlad was saved and Holika was not.

Many people also link Holi to Krishna. In stories from Braj, young Krishna plays with colors with Radha and his friends. Many Hindus say Holi is a time to forgive, make up with friends and enjoy the spring.

words.d: the Hindu spring festival of colors, usually in March
a young prince in the Puranas who stayed devoted to Vishnu

look.title: The Story of Prahlad
look.text: The boy Prahlad kept praying to Vishnu, though his father the king ordered him to stop. His father tried many ways to harm him, but each time Prahlad was protected.

check.why: Holi comes in March, at the end of winter.

check.q: Who tried to burn Prahlad in the story?
check.why: In the Puranas, Prahlad's aunt Holika tried to burn him.

check.q: Which deity do many people link with playing colors on Holi?
check.why: Stories from Braj tell of young Krishna playing colors with Radha and friends.

lessons.title: Navaratri and Durga Puja
lessons.mainIdea: Navaratri, the nine nights, honors the Goddess, and in Bengal it is celebrated as Durga Puja.
reading: For nine nights in the fall, families in Gujarat dance in wide circles, clapping and turning. This dance is called garba. The festival is *Navaratri*, which means nine nights.

Navaratri honors Devi, the Goddess, in her many forms. A text called the Devi Mahatmya tells how the goddess Durga defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Many Hindus see this as the victory of good over evil.
In Bengal, the same season is *Durga Puja*. Families visit tall, beautiful murtis of Durga with her ten arms. The tenth day, Dussehra, is also linked in many places to Rama's victory over Ravana.

words.d: a fall festival of nine nights honoring the Goddess
the Bengali festival honoring the goddess Durga
the Goddess, honored in many forms such as Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati

rows: Arms of Durga in many murtis

check.q: What does Navaratri mean?
check.why: Navaratri means nine nights.

check.q: Whom does Durga defeat in the Devi Mahatmya?
check.why: The Devi Mahatmya tells how Durga defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

check.q: What is the garba?
check.why: Garba is a circle dance performed during Navaratri, especially by Gujarati families.

lessons.title: Janmashtami and Ganesh Chaturthi
lessons.mainIdea: Janmashtami celebrates Krishna's birth, and Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates Ganesha.
reading: At midnight, a temple is packed. A small murti of baby Krishna rests in a decorated cradle. People sing and gently rock it. This is *Janmashtami*, the celebration of Krishna's birth, usually in August or September.

The Bhagavata Purana tells that Krishna was born in a prison in Mathura. His father carried him across a river to safety in Gokul. Many families fast during the day and celebrate at midnight, the hour of his birth.

Soon after comes *Ganesh Chaturthi*. Families bring home a murti of Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity honored as the remover of obstacles. After some days, many carry the murti to water in a joyful parade.

words.d: the festival celebrating the birth of Krishna
the festival honoring Ganesha, the remover of obstacles
the elephant-headed deity Hindus honor as the remover of obstacles

look.title: A Midnight Cradle

look.prompt: Why might a family celebrate at midnight on Janmashtami?

check.q: Which text tells of Krishna's birth in Mathura?

lessons.title: Puja at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Puja is Hindu worship, and many families do it every day at a home shrine.
reading: Early in the morning, a grandmother stands at a small shrine in her kitchen. She lights a lamp, rings a little bell and offers a flower. This is *puja*, Hindu worship.

A home shrine may hold murtis or pictures of Ganesha, Krishna, Shiva, Lakshmi or others. Families offer water, flowers, fruit, incense and light. Many say prayers or sing. Each family does puja in its own way.
Food offered in puja becomes *prasad*. Hindus believe it has been blessed, so it is shared with the family. Many Hindu families in Illinois keep a shrine at home, even in a small apartment.

words.d: Hindu worship, with offerings such as flowers, light and food
food that has been offered in worship and is then shared as a blessing

check.q: Do all families do puja the same way?

lessons.title: Inside a Temple
lessons.mainIdea: In a Hindu temple, priests care for the murtis and lead worship such as arati.
reading: A Hindu temple is called a mandir in Hindi. Inside are shrines, each with a murti. Hindus believe the deity is present in the murti in a special way, so it is bathed, dressed and offered food with great care.

Priests lead worship several times a day. In *arati*, a priest waves a lamp in circles before the murti while people sing and a bell rings. Afterward, many people pass their hands over the flame and touch their eyes.
Seeing the murti is itself important. Hindus call this *darshan*, which means seeing and being seen by the deity. Many visitors come just for darshan, then share prasad and go home.

words.d: a Hindu temple
worship in which a lamp is waved in circles before a murti
seeing and being seen by the deity in a temple or shrine

look.title: Seeing and Being Seen

check.q: What is arati?

check.why: In arati, a lamp is waved in circles before the murti.

check.q: What does darshan mean?
choices: Seeing and being seen by the deity
check.why: Darshan means seeing and being seen by the deity.

check.q: What is a mandir?

lessons.title: The Temple in Lemont
lessons.mainIdea: The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago in Lemont, Illinois, has a Rama temple and serves many families.
reading: The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago stands on a hill in Lemont, Illinois. Its main shrine honors Rama, with Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman. Another building has shrines to other deities, including Ganesha, Shiva and Durga.

Families come from all over the Chicago area. They come for weekly worship, weddings, festivals like Diwali and Navaratri, and classes. The temple helps Hindu Americans keep their traditions and teach them to children.

Visitors are often welcome. Guests take off their shoes, dress modestly, speak quietly and do not touch the murtis. It is polite to ask before taking photos. These simple steps show respect for a place that is holy to others.

words.d: a town southwest of Chicago, home of the Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago
showing care and good manners toward people and the things they hold holy
